newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Caribbean community heads for single market.
newsitem.headline: Caribbean community heads for single market.

text.p: Caribbean leaders said Wednesday that members of the 14-member Caribbean Community had approved major changes to the group's treaty that will allow it to become a single market within two years.
"All discernible aspects of the single market will be in place by 1999," Barbados Prime Minister Owen Arthur told a news conference.

Caricom's members -- Antigua, Bahamas, Barbados, Belize, Dominica, Guyana, Grenada, Jamaica, Montserrat, Surinam, St. Vincent, St. Lucia, St. Kitts, and Trinidad and Tobago -- are convinced forming a single market is vital if the region is to benefit from proposals for hemispheric free trade.

The largest Caricom member, Jamaica, has only about three million residents. United, the bloc represents about six million consumers. In contrast, Mercosur, which groups soutern Latin American nations, represents a market of 204 million people.

Twelve of the 14 Caricom members signed a protocol that allows for the free movement of capital and services and permit Caricom investors to establish themselves freely anywhere in the region, although some land-holding restrictions are expected to apply in the smaller states.
Only St. Lucia and the Bahamas delayed signing.
Arthur also said a common external tariff would be fully implemented by Jan. 1, 1998.

He said seven remaining free trade protocols covering industrial policy, trade policy, transportation, dispute settlements, fair competition, agriculture, and disadvantaged economies and sectors are expected to be signed next year.
But Caricom has not yet fully resolved how it will create a unified capital market, or solved the thorniest problem, creation of a common Caricom currency.
